questionText: The hardness of a ground water sample was found to be 420 mg/L as $CaCO_{3}$ . A softener containing ion exchange resins was installed to reduce the total hardness to 75 mg/L as $CaCO_{3}$ before supplying to 4 households. Each household gets treated water at a rate of 540 L/day. If the efficiency of the softener is 100%, the bypass flow rate (expressed in L/day) is _____________.
explanationHtml:
Total water to be treated
=540×4=2160L/ day  =540 \times 4=2160 \text {L/ day }=540×4=2160L/ day 
Resultant hardness required
=75mg/L =75 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}=75mg/L
Let bypass rate be x L/day having hardness of 420 mg / L
Resultant hardness required
=75mg/LCHmix⁡=CH1Q1+CH2Q2Q75=x×420+(2160−x)02160x=2160×75420=385.7  L/day \begin{aligned} &=75 \mathrm{mg} / L \\ \mathrm{CH}_{\operatorname{mix}} &=\frac{\mathrm{CH}_{1} \mathrm{Q}_{1}+\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{Q}_{2}}{\mathrm{Q}} \\ 75 &=\frac{x \times 420+(2160-x) 0}{2160} \\ x &=\frac{2160 \times 75}{420}=385.7 \; L / \mathrm{day} \end{aligned}CHmix​75x​=75mg/L=QCH1​Q1​+CH2​Q2​​=2160x×420+(2160−x)0​=4202160×75​=385.7L/day​
explanationText: Total water to be treated $=540 \times 4=2160 \text {L/ day }$ Resultant hardness required $=75 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}$ Let bypass rate be x L/day having hardness of 420 mg / L Resultant hardness required $\begin{aligned} &=75 \mathrm{mg} / L \\ \mathrm{CH}_{\operatorname{mix}} &=\frac{\mathrm{CH}_{1} \mathrm{Q}_{1}+\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{Q}_{2}}{\mathrm{Q}} \\ 75 &=\frac{x \times 420+(2160-x) 0}{2160} \\ x &=\frac{2160 \times 75}{420}=385.7 \; L / \mathrm{day} \end{aligned}$

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} S_{\mathrm{r}}+S_{\mathrm{y}} &=n \\ \frac{5}{100}+\frac{V_{\mathrm{w}}}{10^{3} \times 10^{6} \times 1} &=\frac{25}{100} \\ V_{\mathrm{w}} &=0.2 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{m}^{3}=0.2 \mathrm{km}^{3} \end{aligned}$

It was found that in order to achieve 97 percent efficiency, the collector plate area should be 6100 $m^{2}$ . In order to increase the efficiency to 99 percent, the ESP collector plate area (expressed in $m^{2}$ ) would be ______
explanationHtml:
As per Deutsch-Anderson equation, to determine the collection efficiency of the precipitator under ideal conditions,
η=1−e−w(A/Q)η=Collection efficiency of the precipitatorw=Migration velocity, cm/sA=The effective collecting plate area of the precipitator, m2Q=Gas flow through the precipitator, m3/s0.96=1−e−(wQ)×5600                  ...(i)0.97=1−e−(wQ)×6100              ...(ii)\begin{aligned} \eta &=1-e^{-w\left ( A/Q \right )} \\ \eta &=\text{Collection efficiency of the precipitator} \\ w &=\text{Migration velocity,}\: cm/s \\ A &=\text{The effective collecting plate area of the precipitator,}\: m^{2} \\ Q &=\text{Gas flow through the precipitator,}\: m^{3}/s \\ 0.96&=1-e^{-\left ( \frac{w}{Q} \right )\times 5600}\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; ...\left ( i \right ) \\ 0.97 &=1-e^{-\left ( \frac{w}{Q} \right )\times 6100}\; \; \; \; \; \; \; ...\left ( ii \right ) \end{aligned}ηηwAQ0.960.97​=1−e−w(A/Q)=Collection efficiency of the precipitator=Migration velocity,cm/s=The effective collecting plate area of the precipitator,m2=Gas flow through the precipitator,m3/s=1−e−(Qw​)×5600...(i)=1−e−(Qw​)×6100...(ii)​
From both equations,
                        wQ=5.748×10−4\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \frac{w}{Q}=5.748\times 10^{-4}Qw​=5.748×10−4
Now for 99% efficiency plate area required,
0.99=1−e−5.748×10−4×A0.99=1-e^{-5.748\times 10^{-4}\times A}0.99=1−e−5.748×10−4×A
⇒          A=8011.78 m2\Rightarrow \; \; \; \; \; A=8011.78\: m^{2}⇒A=8011.78m2

questionText: In a wastewater treatment plant, primary sedimentation tank (PST) designed at an overflow rate of 32.5 $m^{3}/day/m^{2}$ is 32.5 m long, 8.0 m wide and liquid depth of 2.25 m. If the length of the weir is 75 m, the weir loading rate (in $m^{3}/day/m$ ) is ___________.
explanationHtml:
V0=QBLQ=(32.5m3/d/m2)×32.5×8=8450m3/dWeir length =75m\begin{aligned} V_{0} &=\frac{Q}{B L} \\ Q &=\left(32.5 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\right) \times 32.5 \times 8 \\ &=8450 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d}\\ \text{Weir length }&=75 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}V0​QWeir length ​=BLQ​=(32.5m3/d/m2)×32.5×8=8450m3/d=75m​
∴ \therefore ∴ Weir loading rate,
q=845075=112.67m3/d/m q=\frac{8450}{75}=112.67 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} / \mathrm{m}q=758450​=112.67m3/d/m
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} V_{0} &=\frac{Q}{B L} \\ Q &=\left(32.5 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} / \mathrm{m}^{2}\right) \times 32.5 \times 8 \\ &=8450 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d}\\ \text{Weir length }&=75 \mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Weir loading rate, $q=\frac{8450}{75}=112.67 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{d} / \mathrm{m}$

As two filters are out of service, number of filters working =12-2=10

The new loading rate

Total volume=SW+Cover=(9.125+4.5625)×106 m3=13.6875 million m3\begin{aligned} \text{Total volume} &=SW+Cover \\ &=\left ( 9.125+4.5625 \right )\times 10^{6}\: m^{3} \\ &=13.6875\: million\: m^{3} \end{aligned}Total volume​=SW+Cover=(9.125+4.5625)×106m3=13.6875millionm3​
explanationText: Solid waste generated per day $=2\times 200000=400000\: kg$ Total solid waste generated in 25 years $=400000\times 365\times 25=3.65\times 10^{9}\: kg$ Compaction ratio, $4=\frac{Volume\; before\; compaction}{Volume\; after\; compaction}$ Volume of waste before compaction, $V=\frac{3.65\times 10^{9}}{100}=3.65\times 10^{7}\: m^{3}$ Volume of waste after compaction, $V'=\frac{3.65\times 10^{7}}{4}=9.125\times 10^{6}\: m^{3}$ $\frac{SW+cover}{SW}=\frac{SW}{SW}+\frac{cover}{SW}=1.5$ $\frac{Cover}{SW}=0.5$ $Cover=0.5\times 9.125\times 10^{6}$ $\; \; \; =4.5625\times 10^{6}\: m^{3}$ $\begin{aligned} \text{Total volume} &=SW+Cover \\ &=\left ( 9.125+4.5625 \right )\times 10^{6}\: m^{3} \\ &=13.6875\: million\: m^{3} \end{aligned}$

questionText: Consider a primary sedimentation tank (PST) in a water treatment plant with Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) of 40 $m^{3}/m^2/d$ . The diameter of the spherical particle which will have 90 percent theoretical removal efficiency in this tank is_________ $\mu m$ . Assume that settling velocity of the particle in water described by Stokes' Law. Given: Density of water = 1000 $kg/m^{3}$ ; Density of particle = 2650 $kg/m^{3}$ ; g = 9.81 $m/s^{2}$ ; Kinematic viscosity of water $(v) = 1.10 \times 10^{-6} m^{2}/s$
explanationHtml: % removal =Vs′Vs×100Vs′=0.9×Vs=0.9× Overfiow rate Vs′=0.9×4086400m/s(G−1)gd218v=0.9×4086400d=0.9×40×18pwV86400×(Gs−1)×ρw×g=0.9×40×18×1.1×10−686400×1.64×9.81=2.2576×10−5m=22.576mm\begin{aligned} \text { \% removal } &=\frac{V_{s}^{\prime}}{V_{s}} \times 100 \\ V_{s}^{\prime} &=0.9 \times V_{s} \\ &=0.9 \times \text { Overfiow rate } \\ V_{s}^{\prime} &=\frac{0.9 \times 40}{86400} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \\ \frac{(G-1) g d^{2}}{18 \mathrm{v}} &=\frac{0.9 \times 40}{86400} \\ d &=\sqrt{\frac{0.9 \times 40 \times 18 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{w}} \mathrm{V}}{86400 \times\left(G_{s}-1\right) \times \rho_{\mathrm{w}} \times g}} \\ &=\sqrt{\frac{0.9 \times 40 \times 18 \times 1.1 \times 10^{-6}}{86400 \times 1.64 \times 9.81}} \\ &=2.2576 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{m}=22.576 \mathrm{mm} \end{aligned} % removal Vs′​Vs′​18v(G−1)gd2​d​=Vs​Vs′​​×100=0.9×Vs​=0.9× Overfiow rate =864000.9×40​m/s=864000.9×40​=86400×(Gs​−1)×ρw​×g0.9×40×18pw​V​​=86400×1.64×9.810.9×40×18×1.1×10−6​​=2.2576×10−5m=22.576mm​

questionText: A waste water stream (flow=2 $m^{3}$ /s, ultimate BOD=90 mg/l) is joining a small river (flow=12 $m^{3}$ /s, ultimate BOD=5 mg/l). Both water streams get mixed up instantaneously. Cross sectional area of the river is 50 $m^{2}$ . Assuming the de-oxygenation rate constant, k'=0.25/day the BOD (in mg/l) of the river water, 10 km downstream of the mixing point is

Flow of waste water stream,
Qw=2m3/sec Q_{w}=2 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec}Qw​=2m3/sec
Ultimate BOD,
Yw=90mg/l=90gm/m3 Y_{w}=90 \mathrm{mg} / l=90 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{m}^{3}Yw​=90mg/l=90gm/m3
Flow of river,
QR=12m3/sec Q_{R}=12 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec}QR​=12m3/sec
Ultimate BOD of river,
YR=0.5mg/l=5gm/m3 Y_{R}=0.5 \mathrm{mg} / l=5 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{m}^{3}YR​=0.5mg/l=5gm/m3
BOD of mixture,
Y0=(2×90)+(12×5)2+12=180+6014=24014=17.143gm/m3kD=0.434K=0.434×0.25=0.1085Yt=Y0[1−(10)−k0t]…(i) Area of river =50m2 Flow of river =12m3/sec Stream velocity =1450=0.28m/sec Time taken, t=10km0.28m/s=0.4133 days  \begin{aligned} Y_{0} &=\frac{(2 \times 90)+(12 \times 5)}{2+12} \\ &=\frac{180+60}{14}=\frac{240}{14} \\ &=17.143 \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ k_{D} &=0.434 \mathrm{K} \\ &=0.434 \times 0.25=0.1085 \\ Y_{t} &=Y_{0}\left[1-(10)^{-k_{0} t}\right] &\ldots(i)\\ \text { Area of river } &=50 \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Flow of river } &=12 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \text { Stream velocity } &=\frac{14}{50}=0.28 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \text { Time taken, } & t=\frac{10 \mathrm{km}}{0.28 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}}=0.4133 \text { days } \end{aligned}Y0​kD​Yt​ Area of river  Flow of river  Stream velocity  Time taken, ​=2+12(2×90)+(12×5)​=14180+60​=14240​=17.143gm/m3=0.434K=0.434×0.25=0.1085=Y0​[1−(10)−k0​t]=50m2=12m3/sec=5014​=0.28m/sect=0.28m/s10km​=0.4133 days ​…(i)​

Let x be the no. of microorganisms (M.O.) present initially.

questionMarkup:

On calculation, BOD (i.e. 7 day, 20∘^{\circ}∘C) was found to be 150 mg/L. What would be the 5-day, 20∘^{\circ}∘C BOD (in mg/L)?
Assume value of BOD rate constant (k) at standard temperature of 20∘^{\circ}∘C as 0.23/day (base e). __________
questionText: A student began experiment for determination of 5-day, 20 $^{\circ}$ C BOD on Monday. Since the $5^{th}$ day fell on Saturday, the final DO readings were taken on next Monday. On calculation, BOD (i.e. 7 day, 20 $^{\circ}$ C) was found to be 150 mg/L. What would be the 5-day, 20 $^{\circ}$ C BOD (in mg/L)? Assume value of BOD rate constant (k) at standard temperature of 20 $^{\circ}$ C as 0.23/day (base e). __________
explanationHtml: BOD7=L[1−e−k×t]∴    150=L[1−e−0.23×7]⇒    L=187.54 mg/L∴    BOD5=L[1−e−k×t]=187.539×[1−e−0.23×5]=128.13 mg/L\begin{aligned} BOD_{7} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ \therefore \; \; 150 &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 7} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=187.54\: mg/L \\ \therefore \; \; BOD_{5} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ &=187.539\times \left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 5} \right ] \\ &= 128.13\: mg/L \end{aligned}BOD7​∴150⇒L∴BOD5​​=L[1−e−k×t]=L[1−e−0.23×7]=187.54mg/L=L[1−e−k×t]=187.539×[1−e−0.23×5]=128.13mg/L​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} BOD_{7} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ \therefore \; \; 150 &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 7} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=187.54\: mg/L \\ \therefore \; \; BOD_{5} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ &=187.539\times \left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 5} \right ] \\ &= 128.13\: mg/L \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned} BOD_{7} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ \therefore \; \; 150 &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 7} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=187.54\: mg/L \\ \therefore \; \; BOD_{5} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ &=187.539\times \left [ 1-e^{-0.23\times 5} \right ] \\ &= 128.13\: mg/L \end{aligned}

questionText: A settling tank in a water treatment plant is designed for a surface overflow rate of 30 $\frac{m^{3}}{day\cdot m^{2}}$ . Assume specific gravity of sediment particles = 2.65, density of water ( $\rho= 1000 kg/m^3$ ), dynamic viscosity of water ( $\mu=0.001 N.s/m^2$ ), and Stokes' law is valid. The approximate minimum size of particles that would be completely removed is:
explanationHtml:
To calculate minimum size of particles equating setteling velocity to overflow rate, we get,
V0=Vs⇒    V0=(Gs−1)γWd218μNow     V0=30m2day.m2=3024×60×60ms⇒    3024×60×60=(2.65−1)×9.81×103×d218×0.001\begin{aligned} V_{0} &=V_{s} \\ \Rightarrow\; \; V_{0} &=\frac{\left ( G_{s}-1 \right )\gamma _{W}d^{2}}{18\mu } \\ \text{Now }\; \; V_{0}&=\frac{30m^{2}}{day.m^{2}} \\ &=\frac{30}{24\times 60\times 60}\frac{m}{s} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{30}{24\times 60\times 60}&= \frac{\left ( 2.65-1 \right )\times 9.81\times 10^{3}\times d^{2}}{18\times 0.001}\\ \end{aligned}V0​⇒V0​Now V0​⇒24×60×6030​​=Vs​=18μ(Gs​−1)γW​d2​=day.m230m2​=24×60×6030​sm​=18×0.001(2.65−1)×9.81×103×d2​​
Solving we get,
d=1.965×10−5  m≈0.02 mmd=1.965\times 10^{-5}\; m \approx 0.02\, mmd=1.965×10−5m≈0.02mm
explanationText: To calculate minimum size of particles equating setteling velocity to overflow rate, we get, $\begin{aligned} V_{0} &=V_{s} \\ \Rightarrow\; \; V_{0} &=\frac{\left ( G_{s}-1 \right )\gamma _{W}d^{2}}{18\mu } \\ \text{Now }\; \; V_{0}&=\frac{30m^{2}}{day.m^{2}} \\ &=\frac{30}{24\times 60\times 60}\frac{m}{s} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; \frac{30}{24\times 60\times 60}&= \frac{\left ( 2.65-1 \right )\times 9.81\times 10^{3}\times d^{2}}{18\times 0.001}\\ \end{aligned}$ Solving we get, $d=1.965\times 10^{-5}\; m \approx 0.02\, mm$

explanationHtml: PH=9.25∵PH+POH=14⇒pOH=14−9.25=4.75⇒−log⁡10[OH−]=4.75∴[OH]=1.778×10−5(mollit)∴mollit of OH−=1.778×10−5∴gmlit of OH−=1.778×10−5×17=30.226×10−5=302.6×10−6gm/it∴[OH−]=302.6×10−3mg/lit=0.302mg/lit\begin{aligned} \mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{H}} &=9.25 \\ \because\quad \mathrm{PH}+\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{OH}} &=14 \\ \Rightarrow\quad \mathrm{p}^{OH} &=14-9.25=4.75 \\ \Rightarrow\quad -\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] &=4.75 \\ \therefore \quad [\mathrm{OH}] &=1.778 \times 10^{-5}\left(\frac{\mathrm{mol}}{\mathrm{lit}}\right) \\ \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{mol}}{\mathrm{lit}} \text { of } \mathrm{OH}^{-} &=1.778 \times 10^{-5} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{gm}}{\mathrm{lit}} \text { of } \mathrm{OH}^{-} &=1.778 \times 10^{-5} \times 17 \\ &=30.226 \times 10^{-5} \\ &=302.6 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{it} \\ \therefore \quad \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] &=302.6 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{lit} \\ &=0.302 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{lit} \end{aligned}PH∵PH+POH⇒pOH⇒−log10​[OH−]∴[OH]∴litmol​ of OH−∴litgm​ of OH−∴[OH−]​=9.25=14=14−9.25=4.75=4.75=1.778×10−5(litmol​)=1.778×10−5=1.778×10−5×17=30.226×10−5=302.6×10−6gm/it=302.6×10−3mg/lit=0.302mg/lit​

In an aquifer extending over 150 hectare, the water table was 20m below ground

questionText: In an aquifer extending over 150 hectare, the water table was 20m below ground level. Over a period of time the water table dropped to 23m below the ground level. If the porosity of aquifer is 0.40 and the specific retention is 0.15, what is the change in ground water storage of the aquifer?
explanationHtml:
We know that,
n=Sy+Sr⇒Sy=St−n=0.15−0.40=−0.25 \begin{aligned} n&=S_{y}+S_{r} \\ \Rightarrow\quad S_{y}&=S_{t}-n=0.15-0.40=-0.25 \end{aligned}n⇒Sy​​=Sy​+Sr​=St​−n=0.15−0.40=−0.25​
The negative sign signifies the decrease in storage. Change in volume of aquifer
=150×(23−20)=450ha−m =150 \times(23-20)=450 \mathrm{ha}-\mathrm{m}=150×(23−20)=450ha−m
Specific yield is nothing but the actual volume of water that can be extracted by force of gravity from a unit volume of aquifer.
∴\therefore ∴Change in water storage
=450×0.25=112.5ha−m =450 \times 0.25=112.5 \mathrm{ha}-\mathrm{m}=450×0.25=112.5ha−m
explanationText: We know that, $\begin{aligned} n&=S_{y}+S_{r} \\ \Rightarrow\quad S_{y}&=S_{t}-n=0.15-0.40=-0.25 \end{aligned}$ The negative sign signifies the decrease in storage. Change in volume of aquifer $=150 \times(23-20)=450 \mathrm{ha}-\mathrm{m}$ Specific yield is nothing but the actual volume of water that can be extracted by force of gravity from a unit volume of aquifer. $\therefore$ Change in water storage $=450 \times 0.25=112.5 \mathrm{ha}-\mathrm{m}$

questionMarkup: If the BOD3{BOD}_3BOD3​ of a wastewater sample is 75mg/L and reaction rate constant k (base e) is 0.345 per day, the amount of BOD remaining in the given sample after 10 days is
questionText: If the ${BOD}_3$ of a wastewater sample is 75mg/L and reaction rate constant k (base e) is 0.345 per day, the amount of BOD remaining in the given sample after 10 days is
explanationHtml:
The BOD at any instant is given by,
Lt=L[1−e−kt]⇒    75=L[1−e−0.345]⇒    L=751−0.355⇒    L=116.32 mg/l\begin{aligned} L_{t} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-kt} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \;75&=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.345} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L&=\frac{75}{1-0.355} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=116.32\: mg/l \end{aligned}Lt​⇒75⇒L⇒L​=L[1−e−kt]=L[1−e−0.345]=1−0.35575​=116.32mg/l​
BOD after 10 days,
L10=L[1−e−0.345×10]=116.32×0.968=112.63 mg/l\begin{aligned} L_{10} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.345\times 10} \right ] \\ &=116.32\times 0.968 \\ &=112.63\: mg/l \end{aligned}L10​​=L[1−e−0.345×10]=116.32×0.968=112.63mg/l​
Amount of BOD remaining =L−L0L-L_{0}L−L0​
=116.32−112.63=3.69 mg/l\begin{aligned} &=116.32-112.63 \\ &=3.69\: mg/l \end{aligned}​=116.32−112.63=3.69mg/l​
explanationText: The BOD at any instant is given by, $\begin{aligned} L_{t} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-kt} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \;75&=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.345} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L&=\frac{75}{1-0.355} \\ \Rightarrow \; \; L &=116.32\: mg/l \end{aligned}$ BOD after 10 days, $\begin{aligned} L_{10} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.345\times 10} \right ] \\ &=116.32\times 0.968 \\ &=112.63\: mg/l \end{aligned}$ Amount of BOD remaining = $L-L_{0}$ $\begin{aligned} &=116.32-112.63 \\ &=3.69\: mg/l \end{aligned}$

questionText: An air parcel having 40 $^{\circ}$ C temperature moves from ground level to 500 m elevation in dry air following the "adiabatic lapse rate". The resulting temperature of air parcel at 500m elevation will be

options.html: 35∘C^{\circ}C∘C
38∘C^{\circ}C∘C
41∘C^{\circ}C∘C
44∘C^{\circ}C∘C

explanationHtml:
Dry air cools at the rate of 9.8∘C9.8^{\circ}C9.8∘C per km and it is called dry adiabatic lapse rate. In saturated (wet) air, this rate is calculated to be 6∘C6^{\circ}C6∘C per km and is known as wet adiabatic lapse rate.
Resulting temperature of air
=40−9.8×5001000=40−4.9=35.1∘C=40-9.8\times \frac{500}{1000}=40-4.9=35.1^{\circ}C=40−9.8×1000500​=40−4.9=35.1∘C
explanationText: Dry air cools at the rate of $9.8^{\circ}C$ per km and it is called dry adiabatic lapse rate. In saturated (wet) air, this rate is calculated to be $6^{\circ}C$ per km and is known as wet adiabatic lapse rate.Resulting temperature of air $=40-9.8\times \frac{500}{1000}=40-4.9=35.1^{\circ}C$

questionText: A coastal city produces municipal solid waste (MSW) with high moisture content, high organic materials, low calorific value and low inorganic materials. The most effective and sustainable option for MSW management in that city is
explanationHtml: Incineration can be adopted when the calorific value of the MSW is high. Land fill can be adopted when the density of MSW is high. Since in the given MSW the quality of inorganic material is low, its density is less. Composting can be adopted when the MSW contains high organic content. Barging the MSW into the sea is now a days generaly not used and has become obsolete.

questionText: A horizontal flow primary clarifier treats wastewater in which 10%, 60% and 30% of particles have settling velocities of 0.1 mm/s, 0.2 mm/s and 0.1 mm/s respectively. What would be the total percentage of particles removed if clarifier operates at a Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) of 43.2 $m^{3}/m^{2}.d$ ?
explanationHtml:
Surface overflow rate
=43.2  m3/m2−d=43.2  m/d=43.2×10324×60×60  mm/s=0.5  mm/s\begin{aligned} &=43.2\; m^{3}/m^{2}-d=43.2\; \text{m/d} \\ &=\frac{43.2\times 10^{3}}{24\times 60\times 60}\; \text{mm/s} \\ &=0.5\; \text{mm/s} \end{aligned}​=43.2m3/m2−d=43.2m/d=24×60×6043.2×103​mm/s=0.5mm/s​
It means that particles which have setting velocities more than surface overflow rate will be 100% removed.
∴\therefore∴ Total percentage of particles removed
=30+60×0.20.5+10×0.10.5=30+24=2=56%\begin{aligned} &=30+60\times \frac{0.2}{0.5}+10\times \frac{0.1}{0.5} \\ &=30+24=2=56\% \end{aligned}​=30+60×0.50.2​+10×0.50.1​=30+24=2=56%​
explanationText: Surface overflow rate $\begin{aligned} &=43.2\; m^{3}/m^{2}-d=43.2\; \text{m/d} \\ &=\frac{43.2\times 10^{3}}{24\times 60\times 60}\; \text{mm/s} \\ &=0.5\; \text{mm/s} \end{aligned}$ It means that particles which have setting velocities more than surface overflow rate will be 100% removed. $\therefore$ Total percentage of particles removed $\begin{aligned} &=30+60\times \frac{0.2}{0.5}+10\times \frac{0.1}{0.5} \\ &=30+24=2=56\% \end{aligned}$

questionText: A water treatment plant is required to process 28800 $m^{3}/d$ of raw water (density=1000 kg/ $m^{3}$ , kinematic viscosity= $10^{-6}m^{2}/s$ ). The rapid mixing tank imparts a velocity gradient of $900s^{-1}$ to blend 35 mg/l of alum with the flow for a detention time of 2 minutes. The power input (W) required for rapid mixing is
explanationHtml:
The power input (W) required for rapid mixing is expressed in terms of temporal mean velocity gradient, G, expressed by the equation,
G=[PμV]1/2          ⇒          P=G2μVG=\left [ \frac{P}{\mu V} \right ]^{1/2}\; \; \; \; \; \Rightarrow \; \; \; \; \; P=G^{2}\mu VG=[μVP​]1/2⇒P=G2μV
where μ\muμ=dynamic viscosity of raw water
=kinematic viscosity×density=10−6×103=10−3  N-s/m2G=900  s−t=2  minutes=120  seconds\begin{aligned} &=\text{kinematic viscosity}\times \text{density} \\ &=10^{-6}\times 10^{3}=10^{-3}\; \text{N-s}/m^{2} \\ \text{G} &=900\; s^{-} \\ \text{t}&=2\; \text{minutes}=120\; \text{seconds} \end{aligned}Gt​=kinematic viscosity×density=10−6×103=10−3N-s/m2=900s−=2minutes=120seconds​
Discharge of raw water
                =2880024×60×60=0.33  m3/s\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; =\frac{28800}{24\times 60\times 60}=0.33\; m^{3}/s=24×60×6028800​=0.33m3/s
Volume of water in tank,
            V=0.33×120=40  m3\; \; \; \; \; \; V=0.33\times 120=40\; m^{3}V=0.33×120=40m3
∴          P=(900)2×10−3×40\therefore \; \; \; \; \; P=\left ( 900 \right )^{2}\times 10^{-3}\times 40∴P=(900)2×10−3×40
                =32400  \; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; =32400\;=32400watts
explanationText: The power input (W) required for rapid mixing is expressed in terms of temporal mean velocity gradient, G, expressed by the equation, $G=\left [ \frac{P}{\mu V} \right ]^{1/2}\; \; \; \; \; \Rightarrow \; \; \; \; \; P=G^{2}\mu V$ where $\mu$ =dynamic viscosity of raw water $\begin{aligned} &=\text{kinematic viscosity}\times \text{density} \\ &=10^{-6}\times 10^{3}=10^{-3}\; \text{N-s}/m^{2} \\ \text{G} &=900\; s^{-} \\ \text{t}&=2\; \text{minutes}=120\; \text{seconds} \end{aligned}$ Discharge of raw water $\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; =\frac{28800}{24\times 60\times 60}=0.33\; m^{3}/s$ Volume of water in tank, $\; \; \; \; \; \; V=0.33\times 120=40\; m^{3}$ $\therefore \; \; \; \; \; P=\left ( 900 \right )^{2}\times 10^{-3}\times 40$ $\; \; \; \; \; \; \; \; =32400\;$ watts

questionText: The 5-day BOD of a wastewater sample is obtained as 190 mg/l (with k = 0.01 $h^{-1}$ ). The ultimate oxygen demand (mg/l) of the sample will be
explanationHtml:
The BOD of t days may be given as
Lt=L[1−e−k×t]⇒    190=L[1−e−0.01×24×5]⇒  L=271 mg/l\begin{aligned} L_{t} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; 190 &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.01\times 24\times 5} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; L&= 271\: mg/l \end{aligned}Lt​⇒190⇒L​=L[1−e−k×t]=L[1−e−0.01×24×5]=271mg/l​
explanationText: The BOD of t days may be given as $\begin{aligned} L_{t} &=L\left [ 1-e^{-k\times t} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; \; 190 &=L\left [ 1-e^{-0.01\times 24\times 5} \right ] \\ \Rightarrow \; L&= 271\: mg/l \end{aligned}$

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{pOH} &=-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] \\ \Rightarrow\quad \mathrm{pOH} &=-\log \left(10^{-5.6} \times 10^{-3}\right) \\ \Rightarrow\quad \mathrm{pOH} &=-\log \left(10^{-8.6}\right) \\ \mathrm{pOH}&=8.6\\ \text{BH}\quad \mathrm{pH}+\mathrm{pOH} &=14 \\ \Rightarrow\quad \mathrm{pH} &=14-8.6 \\ \Rightarrow\quad \mathrm{pH} &=5.4 \end{aligned}$

questionText: A completely mixed activated sludge process is used to treat a wastewater flow of 1 million litres per day (1 MLD) having a $BOD_5$ of 200 mg/L. The biomass concentration in the aeration tank is 2000 mg/L and the concentration of the net biomass leaving the system is 50 mg/L. The aeration tank has a volume of 200 $m^3$ . What is the average time for which the biomass stays in the system ?
explanationHtml:
The average time for which the biomass stays in the system is known as sludge age (θc)\left(\theta_{\mathrm{c}}\right)(θc​) and it is given by,
θc= Mass of biomass in the system  Mass of biomass leaving the system per day  \theta_{c}=\frac{\text { Mass of biomass in the system }}{\text { Mass of biomass leaving the system per day }} θc​= Mass of biomass leaving the system per day  Mass of biomass in the system ​
⇒θc=200×103×200050×106 \Rightarrow \theta_{c}=\frac{200 \times 10^{3} \times 2000}{50 \times 10^{6}} ⇒θc​=50×106200×103×2000​
⇒θc=8days \Rightarrow \theta_{c}=8 \text{days}⇒θc​=8days
explanationText: The average time for which the biomass stays in the system is known as sludge age $\left(\theta_{\mathrm{c}}\right)$ and it is given by, $\theta_{c}=\frac{\text { Mass of biomass in the system }}{\text { Mass of biomass leaving the system per day }}$ $\Rightarrow \theta_{c}=\frac{200 \times 10^{3} \times 2000}{50 \times 10^{6}}$ $\Rightarrow \theta_{c}=8 \text{days}$
explanationTex: \theta_{c}=\frac{\text { Mass of biomass in the system }}{\text { Mass of biomass leaving the system per day }}

questionMarkup: 50 g of CO2CO_{2}CO2​ and 25 g of CH4CH_{4}CH4​ are produced from the decomposition of municipal solid waste (MSW) with a formula weight of 120 g. What is the average per capita green house gas production in a city of 1 million people with a MSW production rate of 500 ton/day ?
questionText: 50 g of $CO_{2}$ and 25 g of $CH_{4}$ are produced from the decomposition of municipal solid waste (MSW) with a formula weight of 120 g. What is the average per capita green house gas production in a city of 1 million people with a MSW production rate of 500 ton/day ?
explanationHtml:
We know that both CO2CO_{2}CO2​ and CH4CH_{4}CH4​ are green house gases.
∴\therefore∴ Total green house gases produced by 120 gm of MSW
= 50 g CO2CO_{2}CO2​ +25 g of CH4CH_{4}CH4​=75 gm
500 ton of MSW will produce green house gases
=500×106×75120=312.5×106 g/day\begin{aligned} &=500\times 10^{6}\times \frac{75}{120} \\ &= 312.5\times 10^{6}\: g/day \end{aligned}​=500×106×12075​=312.5×106g/day​
Per capita average production of green house gases
=312.5×1061×106 g/day=312.5 g/day≈313 g/day\begin{aligned} &=\frac{312.5\times 10^{6}}{1\times 10^{6}}\: g/day \\ &=312.5\: g/day\approx 313\: g/day \end{aligned}​=1×106312.5×106​g/day=312.5g/day≈313g/day​
explanationText: We know that both $CO_{2}$ and $CH_{4}$ are green house gases. $\therefore$ Total green house gases produced by 120 gm of MSW= 50 g $CO_{2}$ +25 g of $CH_{4}$ =75 gm500 ton of MSW will produce green house gases $\begin{aligned} &=500\times 10^{6}\times \frac{75}{120} \\ &= 312.5\times 10^{6}\: g/day \end{aligned}$ Per capita average production of green house gases $\begin{aligned} &=\frac{312.5\times 10^{6}}{1\times 10^{6}}\: g/day \\ &=312.5\: g/day\approx 313\: g/day \end{aligned}$

questionMarkup: Two electrostatic precipitators (ESPs) are in series. The fractional efficiencies of the upstream and downstream ESPs for size dpd_{p}dp​ are 80% and 65%, respectively. What is the overall efficiency of the system for the same dpd_{p}dp​ ?
questionText: Two electrostatic precipitators (ESPs) are in series. The fractional efficiencies of the upstream and downstream ESPs for size $d_{p}$ are 80% and 65%, respectively. What is the overall efficiency of the system for the same $d_{p}$ ?
explanationHtml:
Given data: η1=80\eta _{1}=80%;\; \; \eta _{2}=65%η1​=80
Since the efficiency of upstream ESP is 80%, only 20% of the particulate are not removed. These remaining particulates will face the downstream ESP whose efficiency is 65%.
∴\therefore∴ Particulates removed by downstream,
ESP=20×65100=13% ESP=20\times \frac{65}{100}=13\%ESP=20×10065​=13%
The two ESPs are connected in series, therefore the overall efficiency = 80 + 13 = 93%.
explanationText: Given data: $\eta _{1}=80%;\; \; \eta _{2}=65%$ Since the efficiency of upstream ESP is 80%, only 20% of the particulate are not removed. These remaining particulates will face the downstream ESP whose efficiency is 65%. $\therefore$ Particulates removed by downstream, $ESP=20\times \frac{65}{100}=13\%$ The two ESPs are connected in series, therefore the overall efficiency = 80 + 13 = 93%.

options.text: 250 mg/L carbonate hardness and zero non-carbonate hardness

options.html: 250 mg/L carbonate hardness and 100 mg/L non-carbonate hardness
options.text: 250 mg/L carbonate hardness and 100 mg/L non-carbonate hardness

explanationHtml:
Carbonate hardness is equal to the total hardness or alkalinity whichever is lesser.
In this case alkalinity (250 mg/l )is less than total hardness (350 mg/l).
carbonate hardness = 250 mg/l as CaC03CaC0_{3}CaC03​.
Non-carbonate hardness is the total hardness in excess of the alkalinity
i.e Non-carbonate hardness
= Total hardness - alkalinity =350-250
=100mg/L as CaCO3 =100 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}\text{ as }\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}=100mg/L as CaCO3​

Non-carbonate hardness is the total hardness in excess of the alkalinity i.e Non-carbonate hardness = Total hardness - alkalinity =350-250 $=100 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}\text{ as }\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$

questionText: The dispersion of pollutants in atmosphere is maximum when

options.html: environment lapse rate is less than adiabatic lapse rate

options.html: maximum mixing depth is equal to zero

explanationHtml: When the environment lapse rate is more than the adiabatic lapse rate, a rising parcel of warm lighter air (pollutants) will continue to lift up; where as a parcel of heavier cooler air will continue to come down. In such circumstances the environment is unstable and the dispersion of pollutants will be rapid due to marked vertical mixing of the air.

The effect of increase in certain rapid sand filter and influent particle characteristics on time (TBT_{B}TB​) for reaching particle breakthrough (turbidity > \gt> 2.5 NTU) in the effluent, and time (THT_{H}TH​) of reaching terminal head-loss(> \gt> 3 m) across filter bed are given below. Explain the results based on you understanding of filter operation and particle removal mechanisms operative in rapid sand filters. Assume that when one characteristic is changed, all other characteristic remain fixed.



Effect of increase in filter depth (L)
TBT_{B}TB​ : TBT_{B}TB​ will increase since particles in water will have the opportunity to potentially interact with more collectors, and hence the change for particle attachment to a collector is more.
THT_{H}TH​: Since bed depth is more, water is encounter more resistance is passing through the bed. Hence THT_{H}TH​ will decrease.
Effect of increase in superdicial velocity (VsV_{s}Vs​)
TBT_{B}TB​: Since pore velocity is more, the shear forces experianced by collected particles will be more. Hence particle detachment will be more, leading to a decrease in TBT_{B}TB​.
THT_{H}TH​: Since particle loading rate on the filter and rate of particle collection in the filter will increase, the porosity of the filter bed will decrease more rapidly, leading to more rapid head-loss buildup and hence a decrease in THT_{H}TH​.
Effect of increase in influent particle concentration (CoC_{o}Co​)
TBT_{B}TB​: Particle loading rate on the filter, rate of particle collection and hence porosity of the filter bed will decrease more rapidly. Thus pre velocity in the filter bed will increase more rapidly, leading to more rapid particle detachment. This will lead to decrease in TBT_{B}TB​.
THT_{H}TH​: Since particle loading rate on the filter and rate of particle collection in the filter will be increase, the porosity of the filter bed will decrease more rapidly, leading to more rapid head-loss buildup and hence a decrease in THT_{H}TH​.
Effect of increase in floc strength
TBT_{B}TB​: Particle detachment due to shear force will become less prominent leading to increase in TBT_{B}TB​.
THT_{H}TH​: Since particle retention in the filter will be more, the porosity of the filter bed will decline faster leading to faster buildup of head-loss and hence THT_{H}TH​ will decrease.
Effect of increase in collector diameter (d)
TBT_{B}TB​: Increase in collector diameter will mean the presence of a lesser number of collector in the filter media. This will result is lesser number of potential interaction between a particle and a collector. Thus TBT_{B}TB​ is expected to decrease.
THT_{H}TH​: Since lesser number of particle will be collected as mentioned above, the rate of head-loss buildup will be lower, leading to increase in THT_{H}TH​.
Effect of increase in porosity (α\alpha α)
It must be realized that the porosity of the filter media does not depend on particle size, but on grading of particles. Well-graded sand, i.e., with a broader particle size distribution will have less porosity, as compared to poorly graded sand with a narrower particle size distribution.
TBT_{B}TB​ : In case poorly graded sand (with more porosity) is used as the filter media, the influent particles will potentially encounter lesser number of collectors and will not be collected efficiently.Hence TBT_{B}TB​ will decrease.
THT_{H}TH​: Increase in porosity of sand and poor particle collection as described above will result in lower rate of head-loss buildup and hence increase in THT_{H}TH​.
Effect of non-addition of coagulant
TBT_{B}TB​: If no coagulants are added, the particles will be stable and hence will not attach efficiently to the filter media. Hence TBT_{B}TB​ will decrease.
THT_{H}TH​: Since rate of particle clollection in the filter media will be lower as described above, the rate of head-loss buildup will also be lower, leading to an increase in THT_{H}TH​.

questionText: A synthetic sample of water is prepared by adding 100 mg Kaolinite (a clay mineral), 200 mg glucose, 168 mg NaCl, 120 mg $MgSO_{4}$ , and 111 mg $CaCL_{2}$ to 1 litre of pure water. The concentrations of total solids (TS) and fixed dissolved solids (FDS) respectively in the solution in mg/L are equal to
explanationHtml:
Total Solids =100+200+168+120+111=699mg/l\begin{aligned} \text { Total Solids } &=100+200+168+120+111 \\ &=699 \mathrm{mg} / l \end{aligned} Total Solids ​=100+200+168+120+111=699mg/l​
Fixed dissolved solids
= Total Solids − suspended solids=699−100−200=399mg/l \begin{aligned} &=\text{ Total Solids }-\text{ suspended solids}\\ &=699-100-200 \\ &=399 \mathrm{mg} / l \end{aligned}​= Total Solids − suspended solids=699−100−200=399mg/l​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \text { Total Solids } &=100+200+168+120+111 \\ &=699 \mathrm{mg} / l \end{aligned}$ Fixed dissolved solids $\begin{aligned} &=\text{ Total Solids }-\text{ suspended solids}\\ &=699-100-200 \\ &=399 \mathrm{mg} / l \end{aligned}$

explanationHtml:
Large G value with short times tend to produce small, dense flocs, while low G values and long times produce larger, lighter flocs. Since larger, dense flocs are more easily removed in the setting basin, it may be advantageous to vary the G values over the length of the flocculation basin.
The small dense flocs produced at high G values subsequently combine into larger flocs at the lower G values. Reduction in G values by a factor of 2 from the influent end to the effluent end of the flocculator has been shown to be effective.

questionText: The present population of a community is 28000 with an average water consumption of 4200 $m^{3}$ /d. The existing water treatment plant has a design capacity of 6000 $m^{3}$ /d. It is expected that the population will increase to 44000 during the next 20 years. The number of years from now when the plant will reach its design capacity, assuming an arithmetic rate of population growth, will be
explanationHtml:
Assuming arithmetic rate of growth of population.
Increase in population per year
=44000−2800020=800 =\frac{44000-28000}{20}=800=2044000−28000​=800
Discharge required to reach design capacity
=6000−4200=1800m3/d =6000-4200=1800 m^{3} / d=6000−4200=1800m3/d
Present average water consumption per head per day
=420028000=0.15m3 =\frac{4200}{28000}=0.15 \mathrm{m}^{3}=280004200​=0.15m3
Increase in water consumption each year
=0.15×800=120m3/day =0.15 \times 800=120 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{day}=0.15×800=120m3/day
∴ \therefore ∴ No. of years required to reach design capacity
=1800120=15 years  =\frac{1800}{120}=15 \text { years }=1201800​=15 years
explanationText: Assuming arithmetic rate of growth of population. Increase in population per year $=\frac{44000-28000}{20}=800$ Discharge required to reach design capacity $=6000-4200=1800 m^{3} / d$ Present average water consumption per head per day $=\frac{4200}{28000}=0.15 \mathrm{m}^{3}$ Increase in water consumption each year $=0.15 \times 800=120 \mathrm{m}^{3} / \mathrm{day}$ $\therefore$ No. of years required to reach design capacity $=\frac{1800}{120}=15 \text { years }$
